title: Pull request workflow

overview.what:
A Pull Request (PR) is a request to merge your code changes into the main project. Instead of adding your code directly to the final project, you ask the team to review it first.

```python
# Step 1: You make a copy (branch) of the project.
main_project = ['homepage']
my_branch = main_project.copy()

# Step 2: You add your new feature.
my_branch.append('login_page')

# Step 3: You create a PR. The team reviews it. If approved, it is merged.
main_project = my_branch
print(main_project) # Output: ['homepage', 'login_page']
```

A PR acts like a security gate. It stops bad code from breaking the main project. The most important rule: **A PR is a conversation, not just a merge button.** You push your code, the team checks it, you fix any issues, and then it gets merged.
overview.why: It keeps the main codebase safe. It allows the team to spot errors before they reach users.

why_learning_this: Every modern software team uses pull requests to manage changes.
It is how you will submit your work in your first job.

common_mistakes.title: Huge pull requests
common_mistakes.explanation: Putting too many changes in one PR makes it impossible to review. Keep PRs small and focused on one feature.

common_mistakes.title: Ignoring feedback
common_mistakes.explanation: A PR is a discussion. If a reviewer asks for a change, you must update your branch and reply. Do not just close it or merge anyway.

recall_questions.q: Explain a pull request in your own words, as if to a classmate.
recall_questions.answer: A pull request is a way to ask your team to review your code before it gets added to the main project.

recall_questions.q: Why is it important to create a pull request instead of adding code directly?
recall_questions.answer: It acts as a security gate to keep the main code safe and lets the team catch errors before they affect users.

recall_questions.q: What happens if the team finds an issue in your pull request?
recall_questions.answer: You fix the issue by updating your branch. A PR is a conversation, so you make the changes and reply.

understanding_checks.question: What does this print? (This simulates a PR that is NOT merged yet.)
understanding_checks.why: Because `my_work` is a copy (a branch), changes to it do not affect the main `project` until they are officially merged.

understanding_checks.question: If you push 3 new commits to your branch after opening a PR, what happens to the PR?
understanding_checks.answer: The PR updates automatically to include the new commits.
understanding_checks.why: A PR tracks the branch, not just a static set of commits. Any new commits on that branch become part of the ongoing PR.

practice_tasks.title: Simulate a rejected PR
practice_tasks.prompt: Given this code that simulates a PR, modify it so that the PR is REJECTED and the main branch is not updated.
practice_tasks.starter_code:
main_branch = ['v1']
my_branch = main_branch.copy()
my_branch.append('bad_code')
# Merge happens here
main_branch = my_branch
print(main_branch)
practice_tasks.solution:
main_branch = ['v1']
my_branch = main_branch.copy()
my_branch.append('bad_code')
# PR is rejected, merge does not happen
print(main_branch)
